answer.summary: Orosz’s practical approach is to create external structure: set recurring deadlines, protect focus time, and make it easier to start by committing to a short distraction-free session. He also uses a shared workspace for some social structure. [S2, S3, S6]

sections.heading: Create deadlines and a recurring cadence
sections.content: Orosz says deadlines work because pressure helps him follow through. For his newsletter, he built a schedule that gives him writing pressure on most days: he starts the next issue Wednesday, writes Thursday’s issue on Thursday, and begins the following Tuesday issue on Friday. He says knowing paying readers have expectations also helps. As a synthesis for independent work, set specific, recurring deliverables rather than relying only on motivation. [S3, S4]

sections.heading: Make starting small and remove distractions
sections.content: When he struggles to begin, Orosz sets a 20-minute timer and commits to doing only the task during that time. He blocks distracting sites—using a script that disables access and must be run again to unblock them—and says that after a few minutes he often gets into focused work. He also found the Pomodoro method’s 25-minute intervals useful for a few months, and says the Centered app helped him with focused time. [S1, S2, S4, S5]

sections.heading: Add structure around the work
sections.content: Orosz says having a mostly empty calendar gives him more focus time and fewer meetings. He also compensates for missing workplace interaction by working in a shared office, where he can say hello and make small talk. These are options he describes from his own experience, not guarantees. He notes that when he has no pressure he may not do much, but wonders whether that sometimes means he needs to rest; he says he has not fully figured that out. [S2, S3, S6]
